https://www.dw.com/en/india-anger-over-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IYSh Students have been protesting in Ranchi for over two weeks Image: Somnath Sen/ANI Advertisement Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process. Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly. The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters. The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi. Cockroach revolution turns on India's leader To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led " Cockroach " protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike . Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated. "The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW. He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned. But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs. At least six protesters are on hunger strike in Jharkhand Image: ANI News/IMAGO What sparked the protests in Jharkhand? The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July. Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated. Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure. But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem. Devendra Nath Mahto has been on hunger strike for nine days and has lost more than 10 kilograms [FILE: August 4, 2026] Image: Somnath Sen/ANI What are the protesters' demands? The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated. They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery. The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies. The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken. "The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW. Anger at civil service recruitment exams in Jharkhand has been simmering for years Image: ANI Photo Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India? The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers. That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan . CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters. But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined. Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi. "Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system ," Bora told DW. "They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future." Student leader Neha Bora (wearing glasses) joined the protesters in Ranchi Image: Yousuf Sarfaraz/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights. Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition. "Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW. "The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added. Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12. "The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment. India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media , hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession. The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission. But India's youth are refusing to stop there . Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure . For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest. "We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/10/shad.text: Syrian travellers crossing into Lebanon pay up to 60 times the official entry fee to brokers, fixers and travel agencies behind a profitable parallel market around Lebanese border procedures that have tightened sharply since Bashar al-Assad's fall in December 2024.A driver working the Damascus-Beirut route, speaking to Euronews on condition of anonymity for security reasons, described a system in which travel agencies in the Syrian capital, paperwork fixers at the crossing and partners in Beirut sell packaged entry solutions to Syrians who cannot navigate the official process alone.Lebanon's General Security Directorate charges up to $75 in official fees. The actual cost borne by travellers, according to Euronews' sources, is nowhere near that figure.A 48-hour stay arranged through the network costs $180, a week costs around $260 and a month runs to $400. A six-month option — currently suspended — was priced at $1,500, while arranging an annual residence costs approximately $4,700.The difference between the official fee and what travellers actually pay goes to the fixers as "bribes" or "kickbacks" to facilitate paperwork and bypass requirements such as proving cash reserves, presenting a hotel booking, or producing an onward airline ticket.The process runs on enforced discretion. Travellers must not reveal to Lebanese General Security personnel that a driver or agency arranged their paperwork."Revealing this relationship could lead to the driver's arrest and a ban on his entering Lebanese territory," the source said.Under what he described as the "tourist group" arrangement, travellers must also surrender their passport or identity card to a guarantor or company representative for the duration of the stay, to be returned on departure. Those granted a "free document" arrangement can keep their papers.Lebanon's punishing penaltiesEven categories of travellers who should theoretically benefit from smoother procedures are charged.Holders of professional union cards, first-category commercial registrations or electronic visas for third countries are asked to pay a $60 "service fee" at the border on top of other costs, with waiting times that remain long and permitted stays that are kept short — 15 days for traders and union members, 24 hours for transit travellers.The penalties for overstaying are punishing. Exceeding a one-month permit by a single day results in a $60 fine and a one-year ban from Lebanon. Violating a six-month residence limit costs $270 in fines, rising the longer the overstay continues.Lebanon hosts an estimated 1.5 million Syrian refugees, the highest per capita refugee population in the world relative to the host country's size.Lebanese authorities have cited pressure on public services, the labour market and the broader refugee dossier as justification for restricting Syrian entry.The procedures have tightened over several years and have intensified since the fall of al-Assad's regime, which has drawn significant numbers of Syrians back toward the border.The Syrian side of the crossing has become easier since December 2024. Checkpoints run by the Fourth Division and other Assad-era security units — notorious for extortion and harassment — have gone. The complications are now mostly on the Lebanese side.Infrastructure issues not helpingPhysical damage to infrastructure has added to the journey's cost. Israeli air strikes before al-Assad's fall destroyed the Daboussieh and Arida crossings, which remain closed.Vehicles from Syria's coastal cities must now travel a significantly longer inland route through Homs, Qusayr, Hermel and Baalbek before entering Lebanon.The Jisr Qamar-Bekaa crossing is open only to pedestrians after sustaining damage. A car from Damascus to Beirut — 114 kilometres — costs around $100 one way.The same journey from Latakia, forced along the detour, costs roughly $250, or $500 return, over what becomes up to 800 kilometres of travel.The source said he and colleagues now frequently cross with only one or two passengers, whereas previously they would have filled a vehicle.Before 2014, he recalled, a Syrian could present an identity card at the border and receive six months' entry.He said he hoped movement between the two countries would ease again, restoring business to drivers and opening up travel and tourism that the current system has effectively priced out of reach for many Syrians.Euronews could not independently verify all figures provided by the source. Lebanese authorities had not responded to a request for comment at the time of publication.

https://www.thetelegraphandargus.co.uk/n.text: Best Bakery 2026 Business Food and drink Leisure Frizinghall House of Bread in running for Bradford's best bakery 2026 By Amelia Short T&A Trainee Reporter Share 0 Comments House of Bread's Barbara Laszkowska (Image: Newsquest) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. CUSTOMERS queue down the street at a Bradford district bakery "come rain or shine", according to its owners. House of Bread, located on Bradford Road in Frizinghall, has been named as one of the finalists in our best bakery competition. Sara Laszkowski, who co-owns the bakery with her siblings, said: "We’re so happy to hear that we’ve made the top 10. "We feel over the moon and really grateful. "We know how lucky we are with the community around this bakery, so having that support recognised makes it even more special. "There's something lovely about doing a job you genuinely love and then having the people around you say they think you're doing it well. "So, thank you to everyone who nominated us, whether you've been coming since day one or only found us last week." It's family business House of Bread, which opened in March 2017 , is run by five siblings who each manage different parts of the business. Ms Laszkowski said: "It all started with our mum, Barbara. "Baking has always been at the centre of our family and that's down to her. "Every family gathering came with a table full of homemade cakes and many of those recipes have been passed down through generations and are still baked here today. "What began as sourdough for family and friends grew as more people asked for it, which led to supplying a few local shops, and eventually to opening a bakery of our own." A bake from House of Bread (Image: UGC) 11 varieties of sourdough The idea for the business began with a search for the perfect sourdough loaf. "We just couldn't find a loaf we loved, one that tasted incredible and was made with nothing more than flour, water and salt, so we thought we'd have a go at making our own," Ms Laszkowski said. The bakery now produces 11 varieties of sourdough and a wide selection of pastries, all made by hand in small batches. Ms Laszkowski said: "We love weaving our Polish heritage into what we bake, whether that's a traditional recipe like jagodzianki (a sweet bun filled with blueberry) or just the flavours we grew up with, but we're proper foodies too and take inspiration from all over the world. "We only want to make food we'd be excited to eat ourselves. "We're always trying new things, but every bake has to be genuinely delicious and made to a really high standard." Importance of customer base She said: "customers are at the heart of everything we do. "Rain or shine, they’re out there queuing for their weekly bread and sweet treats and on a busy day that queue can stretch right to the end of the street. "We're so grateful for everyone's patience and support. "Winning would mean the world, mostly because it would come from the community that has backed us the whole way." Readers have until September 12 to vote for their winner. All you need to do is pick up a copy of the Telegraph & Argus and fill out the voting coupon in the paper. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, says there has been ‘a reaction amongst the community’ to material such as One Nation’s cartoons. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, says there has been ‘a reaction amongst the community’ to material such as One Nation’s cartoons. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images Australian security and counter-terrorism AFP boss says politicians’ heated rhetoric is fuelling threats against MPs Commissioner Krissy Barrett says women are more often singled out, often with threats of sexual violence Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Sat 24 Oct 2026 23.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 23.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia’s top federal law enforcement official has drawn a direct link between politicians’ rhetoric and threats and abuse being directed at leaders. The safety of elected representatives at all levels has been thrown into the spotlight after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly deliberate attacked outside her Wangaratta electoral office. Haines remains in a serious but stable condition at the Alfred hospital in Melbourne, following her double leg amputation. The tragic events of the past week have shown Australians who we are – and it’s a long way from our image of ourselves | Julianne Schultz Read more The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said there was no doubt the threat environment had changed for politicians. “When I start work every morning, one of the first things I do is read a report … [that] summarises all of the threats that have been reported to the AFP over the last 24 hours,” she told the ABC’s Insiders program. “Now, some days that report is pages and pages long.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The commissioner said she wasn’t interested in policing free speech or intervening in political discourse. “But I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse,” she added. The move from the sending of physical hate mail to online threats had played a significant role in the increasing volume of worrying material, while also highlighting the influence of inflammatory political imagery and language. “We do see where there is particular political conflict or discourse occurring … it does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it’s very immediate,” Barrett said. Past One Nation cartoons depicting political figures, including the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, being hit by cars or buses have resurfaced in the days since the alleged attack on Haines. The AFP commissioner said there was “a reaction amongst the community” to material such as the cartoons. View image in fullscreen Tributes outside the Wangaratta electoral office of independent federal MP Helen Haines on 20 October. Photograph: James Ross/EPA The policing agency, which is responsible for protecting federal politicians and office-holders, has held a number of emergency safety briefings with parliamentarians since Monday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t have Read more Male and female MPs were targeted equally with threats and abuse, Barrett said, but women were more often singled out individually, often with threats of sexual violence. “My hope is that this really causes people to pause and have a think about what’s happening in this country and the impact of that,” she said. “And if this is not the incident, then what is?” Federal MPs from across the political spectrum have acknowledged the difficulty in balancing their personal security and access to voters. “As a local MP, I don’t want to stop going to community events,” Liberal frontbencher Ted O’Brien told News24 on Sunday. “That open access is a cornerstone of democracy. We’re particularly good at it in Australia. We can’t take away grassroots politics.” Labor minister Catherine King said she has been contending with the deteriorating safety for some time. “It is when, not if, that something will happen to one of us and we’ve been saying that certainly for the last five years or so,” she said. “I had a mobile caravan for almost 25 years. I don’t use that now because it doesn’t have a second exit point. “If someone did kick off and I’m trapped in the van, it’s very hard to deal with that.” Explore more on these topics Australian security and counter-terrorism Helen Haines Australian police and policing Melbourne Australian politics Violence against women and girls news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters
